title: Video Editing
summary: Learn video editing from story to export: editing as storytelling, software, formats and organisation, cutting techniques, sound and music rights, colour, titles and captions, and exporting, client work and careers.
audience: Beginner editors, content creators, small businesses, churches and NGOs making video

body.p: Video editing is the craft of selecting, arranging and refining shots, sound and graphics into a finished piece that tells a story or delivers a message. Editors decide what the audience sees, for how long, and in what order. Good editing is often invisible: viewers feel the rhythm and emotion without noticing the cuts.

list: Short social videos, adverts and music videos.
Documentaries, news packages and interviews.
Films, series and web shows.
Event videos such as weddings, conferences and church services.
Training and explainer videos for businesses and NGOs.

body.p: Most pieces follow a beginning (hook and setup), middle (development and tension) and end (resolution and call to action). On social media the first two or three seconds decide whether viewers keep watching, so start with the strongest moment, question or image.

body.tip: Before you touch the timeline, write one sentence saying what the video must make the viewer feel or do.

list: Free and low-cost editors include DaVinci Resolve, CapCut, Shotcut, Kdenlive and phone apps; professional tools include Adobe Premiere Pro and Final Cut Pro.
A computer with enough memory and storage matters more than the brand of software; editing on a phone is fine for short social content.
Resolution: 1920 x 1080 (Full HD) is a 16 : 9 frame; vertical video for phones is 1080 x 1920, a 9 : 16 frame.
Frame rate: 25 frames per second (fps) is standard for broadcast in most of Africa; one minute at 25 fps is 25 x 60 = 1500 frames. 30 fps is common online.
Bitrate controls quality and file size: at 8 megabits per second, a 10-minute (600 s) video is about 8 x 600 / 8 = 600 megabytes.

body.p: Create folders for footage, audio, music, graphics and exports. Rename clips clearly, back up footage on two drives before editing, and keep the project file with the media. Disorganisation is the most common cause of lost work and missed deadlines.

body.tip: Match the project frame rate to your footage to avoid jerky motion.

steps: Watch and log all footage, marking the best takes.
Build a rough cut: put the story in order without worrying about details.
Refine to a fine cut: tighten timing, remove pauses and choose the strongest moments.
Lock the picture, then finish sound, colour and graphics.

list: Straight cut: one shot directly follows another; the most common.
Cutaway or B-roll: shots that illustrate what someone is saying, also hiding jumps in an interview.
Jump cut: a cut within the same shot, used deliberately for energy in vlogs.
J-cut and L-cut: audio from the next shot starts early (J) or audio from the previous shot continues (L), making conversations flow.
Match cut: linking two shots by similar shapes or movement.

body.p: The 30-degree rule says that when cutting between two shots of the same subject, the camera angle should change by at least 30 degrees, or the cut looks like a mistake. Cutting on action, in the middle of a movement, makes cuts smoother.

body.tip: If a shot does not move the story forward, cut it, even if it is beautiful.

body.p: Audiences forgive average pictures more readily than bad sound. Clear dialogue is the first priority.

list: Record clean audio on set with a lapel or shotgun microphone; fixing bad sound later is hard.
Keep dialogue levels consistent, peaking around -6 dB, and never let audio clip (hit 0 dB).
Use background music to set mood, lowering it under speech (ducking).
Add sound effects and room tone to make scenes feel real.
Remove background noise carefully; too much processing makes voices sound robotic.

body.p: Using popular songs without a licence can get videos blocked, muted or removed, and may lead to legal claims. Use royalty-free or licensed music libraries, music you have permission to use, or commission local musicians. Always keep proof of licences.

body.tip: Edit to the beat of the music in montages; cutting on beats makes sequences feel energetic and intentional.

list: Colour correction fixes problems: white balance, exposure and matching shots so they look consistent.
Colour grading creates a mood or style, such as warm and golden or cool and dramatic.
Check skin tones carefully; they are what viewers notice most, and all skin tones should look natural.
Use scopes (waveform and vectorscope) rather than trusting a single screen.

body.p: Use clear, readable fonts, keep text on screen long enough to read twice, and stay within safe margins so text is not cut off on phones or TVs. Lower thirds introduce speakers by name and role. Captions or subtitles are essential: many people watch social video with the sound off, and captions make content accessible to deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers.
Keep a consistent visual style for a brand: the same fonts, colours and logo placement across videos.

body.tip: Read every title aloud before export; spelling mistakes in names destroy credibility.

list: Export with settings that suit the platform: for example H.264 MP4 at 1080p for most online platforms.
Export vertical (9 : 16) versions for phone-first platforms and square or horizontal versions where needed.
Watch the whole export before sending; check sound, spelling and black frames.
Deliver with a clear file name, such as ClientName_Project_v3_1080p.mp4, and keep version numbers.

body.p: Agree on the brief, length, deadlines, number of revision rounds and price in writing. A 3 minute 20 second video is 200 seconds; at 25 fps that is 5000 frames, a useful way to understand why changes late in a project take time. Charge for extra revisions beyond what was agreed.

Editors work for production houses, broadcasters, agencies, churches, NGOs and as freelancers. Build a showreel of your best 60 to 90 seconds, keep learning, and network with directors and camera operators.

body.tip: Deliver on time every time; reliability wins repeat clients as much as creativity does.
